utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, after the summer recess, to everyone in this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, this is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Registrar, since we have a little bit of a different teams in front of us, I exceptionally would like to ask the parties to present themselves for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Alan Tieger and Mark Harmon with Carmela Javier, case manager, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: David Josse, Your Honour. I've got Mr. Stephen Karganovic, our case manager, and assisting me, Ms. Kelly Pitcher and Ms. Hellen Reynolds who has not been in this courtroom before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Welcome in this courtroom, Ms. Reynolds. Mr. Josse, do I understand that lead counsel will not be present today?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- then today, the main item on our agenda will be that the Chamber will hear any submissions under Rule 98 bis by the parties. But before I give an opportunity to do that, I'd first like to give a decision on the 8th batch of 92 bis witnesses which was still pending and where some new submissions were made. Therefore, I now deliver this decision on the 8th batch of 92 bis witnesses. I briefly recall that the Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's motion for the admission of 92 bis evidence filed on the 6th of June 2003, known as the 7th motion, and the Prosecution's 15th motion dated the 20th of May 2005, which consolidates the remaining 92 bis matters for the Prosecution's case. Is there any problem, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My computer screen is not working, Your Honour. I was going to wait until after Your Honour delivered his judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll then continue with the decision and perhaps at the same time some technician can look at your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore I now continue delivering the decision. This last batch of Prosecution evidence at this stage of the case -- this is the last batch of Prosecution evidence at this stage of the case and it is therefore desirable to dispose of the matter prior to the Rule 98 bis submissions. Mr. Registrar, may I ask you to hand out to the parties a list showing the names of the 92 bis witnesses and related material which is admitted into evidence by virtue of today's decision. One of these witnesses is protected and therefore this handout is to be filed under seal. I will now deliver the Chamber's decision concerning these witnesses. The Chamber has as usual gone through all the proffered material, making its own assessment of the suitability of the material for admission. In relation to witnesses Zujo and Mesic, on the 15th of July, the Prosecution reviewed and resubmitted the material as requested by the Chamber in its oral decision of the 28th of June in a clearer and more ordered form, cutting down the number of documents. However, the Defence still expresses difficulties with certain portions of the material presented. These concerns are found in the Defence's e-mail response of the 1st of August 2005. The Defence notes that the material includes numerous parts signed by people other than Zujo and Mesic. However, the Chamber does not share the Defence's opinion that the material must be clearly divided into material attributed to one of the other of the two witnesses. Where such documents are associated with the investigations that Zujo and Mesic were involved in, it is appropriate to admit them with the reports because they may be said to form part of the reports which were the collective work of several people. This does not mean that persons other than Zujo and Mesic are being admitted as 92 bis witnesses. It merely means that documents made by those other people are admitted through Zujo and Mesic and are treated accordingly, in other words, as documentary evidence connected with the expert reports. The primary evidence is the work that Zujo and Mesic authored or co-authored to the extent that this can be determined. That is the evidence of the two witnesses which is admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis. This 92 rule -- to this Rule 92 bis decision. The Defence raised additional issues in an e-mail which was sent one day after the e-mail we just referred to. They included the observation that certain documents in the submitted material contained tendentious assertions. The Chamber does agree with the Defence that, for example, reference to the "Serb aggressor" are vague and likely to be given little weight. However, they are not a reason for non-admission. The statement of many 92 bis witnesses admitted thus far contained similar vague references. This goes to weight. The Chamber has noted that several autopsy results do not reliably determine or in some cases do not in themselves provide sufficient information for making a determination about the ethnicity of the victims. Evidence of this kind may be insufficient to support any allegation in the indictment and will be treated accordingly. However, despite the apparent lack or relevance of some of the evidence, it is more efficient at this late stage of the proceedings to admit that evidence and ignore the uninformative portions later on rather than to try to single those portions out now and remove them from the proffered reports. The other substantial issues raised by the Defence in the aforementioned e-mail have been covered by what we have said until now. The evidence of Zujo and Mesic is therefore admitted, subject to the above qualifications. We now turn to Witness Dobraca. The Defence has no objection to the admission of the requested evidence as shown in the handout. The Chamber agrees that it meets the 92 bis admissibility requirements. It is therefore admitted. In respect of Witness Kaiser, the Chamber already admitted into evidence the report of this expert witness but not yet the transcript. The Chamber invited the Prosecution to explain whether it intended to seek admission of the transcripts in their entirety. Prosecution informed the Chamber that it sought admission only of the highlighted parts of the transcripts of the 1996 Rule 61 hearing and that it was withdrawing the Blaskic transcript from its application. The Defence has no objection to the admission of the Rule 61 transcript. This has been checked by the Chamber and the highlighted parts of the transcript are now admitted into evidence. I now turn to Witness Wright. By its oral decision on the 6th batch of Rule 92 bis witnesses on the 28th of June, the Chamber admitted into evidence both requested transcripts of the 26th and the 29th of May 2000 but it was subsequently noted that no portion of the 29th of May transcript and only a few pages of the 26th May transcript were highlighted. After clarification by the Prosecution, it is now clear that the Prosecution sought the admission only of the highlighted portion of the 26th of May transcript and not of any part of the 29th May transcript. The highlighted parts of the 26th of May transcript are the items in evidence and the whole of the 29th of May transcript is withdrawn from the evidence. Mr. Registrar is kindly requested to delete this item from the list of exhibits in this case. Lastly, Witness 674, in the 15th motion the Prosecution requested the Chamber to admit a corrective statement dated 2003 to an original statement not listed for admission, dated 1998. On the 12th of July, the Prosecution filed a clarification to the Prosecution's 15th motion and informed the Chamber of its wish to request the admission of the 1998 statement as well. The Defence did not object to either one of the statements being admitted and the Chamber has decided to admit both in evidence. The Chamber requests the Prosecution to submit the material admitted through this decision to Mr. Registrar. In due course, Mr. Registrar will assign exhibit numbers to these items and inform the parties and the Chamber. This ends the Chamber's decision on the 8th batch of 92 bis witnesses. Mr. Josse, as you may have noticed, reference was made a couple of times to e-mail submissions which of course are not registered in any way. The Chamber briefly summarised what was the core of these e-mail submissions. I can however imagine that the Defence would insist on having the whole of these e-mails setting out their position being filed in such a way that if need would ever than an Appeals Chamber or at a later stage we could rely on those e-mails rather than have them lost somewhere. I would like you to consider whether, in view of the decision given by the Chamber, you think that the Defence position is sufficiently clarified in the decision itself, if the reference is clear enough; if not, usual invited to make an application or to ask the Chamber to have these e-mails as part of the proceedings and file them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's very helpful, Your Honour. I'll obviously discuss it with Mr. Stewart who I can tell the Court dealt with the submissions in relation to those particular witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then unless there would be any other procedural issue to be raised at this very moment, the Chamber is willing to hear any submissions the parties would like to make in respect of the possibility of entering a judgement of acquittal under Rule 98 bis. And I think, Mr. Josse, that I follow the -- well, tradition is a too much at this moment, since Rule 98 bis has been amended quite recently, but at least I follow the practice in other Chambers if I give you first an opportunity to make whatever oral submissions would you like to make in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was aware that I was likely to have to go first. Before I begin, having had a brief conversation with Mr. Krajisnik this morning, he asked me to make it clear to the Chamber that he asserts that in his view, the Prosecution have failed to substantiate their case and that the whole of the indictment should be dismissed. He understands that I'm going to now make some specific legal submissions for his benefit, as well as anyone else's. I of course make it clear that anything I say in no way amounts to a concession so far as Mr. Krajisnik and the Defence are concerned. Your Honour, the first matter that I invite the Chamber to consider is whether in fact the accused is prejudiced by the change in the Rule. The Court is familiar with the fact that Rule 98 bis was in fact amended on the 4th of December of last year, in other words, in the middle of this trial. The Court is also aware of the formulation of words in Rule 6(D) of the Rules which I will briefly read, if I may - so it's Rule 6(D) of both the old and indeed the existing Rules - which says "An amendment shall enter into force seven days after the date of issue of an official Tribunal document containing the amendment but shall not operate to prejudice the rights of the accused or of a convicted or acquitted person in any pending case." Now, to my knowledge, the matter was raised by the Trial Chamber in the case of Oric, where a similar issue arose, namely the Rule was changed I think shortly after that case had begun, in fact. But it matters not. I've got a small bundle of documents that I'm going to hand up. Perhaps I could hand them all up in one go. It would be easiest. It includes a reference to the discussion, if I can put it like that, between Judge Agius and counsel in the Oric case. Perhaps I could hand those out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you hand out the whole lot of material so that we don't have to distribute them again at a later stage, all the documents. And it was quite helpful, Mr. Josse, to inform the Chamber prior to this hearing what material you would like to distribute so that we could already have a some look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. I have not produced the whole of what amounted to quite a lengthy exchange between Judge Agius and counsel in that case. There are two extracts that I want to deal with. The first is - and there aren't a lot of documents there - if Your Honour looks at the bottom of one of the pages it says page 7879.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At page 7879, in fact let me tell the Court, is towards the end of what was a lengthy exchange. In fact what happened was this: Judge Agius outlined what he felt was the correct new procedure. He heard submissions from the parties. There was then a short break, in fact and after the break he came back into court. And at line 11, he says that there was another matter he needed to mention, and this relates to the retroactive application of the amended Rule. You know as much as we do that we have Rule 60 of the Rules which provides, and I won't read it out again, Your Honour. We then go to line 17. Judge Agius continues, "I have not heard any submissions, and I would have expected those submissions to come from my right side." I think he means the Defence. Mr. Jones on behalf of the accused says, "Yes." The learned Judge continues, "I have not heard any submissions that -- to the effect that the application of the current Rule 98 bis would prejudice the rights of the accused." And Mr. Jones says, "Yes." And for the record I should confirm that we don't wish, we wouldn't say that it prejudices the accused's right. And so clearly on behalf of the accused Oric, Mr. Jones was not taking the point. However, in this case, we contend that the accused is so prejudiced. Your Honour, there are two ways I wish to illustrate that. The old Rule clearly allowed for a comprehensive review of all matters contained in the indictment. By way of example are the schedules which it appears is clear from a number of cases, which I could if need be cite, were reviewed entry by entry, line by line. And if it is accepted by the Defence that the new Rule does not envisage that and clearly doesn't allow it. I mean, it would be absurd to allow oral applications in relation to that because it would be an extremely ungainly and very difficult to manage and take an awfully long time. It's submitted that on this point alone, the Defence can illustrate the prejudice because there can be little question that if a specific line or part of the schedule were removed or deleted under the old Rule 98 bis the Defence would be better off. We contend that's the case for two reasons. Firstly, because it means of course that the accused and the Defence wouldn't have to worry about that particular line, wouldn't have to contemplate calling evidence in relation to it as part of the accused's case, and secondly and perhaps more importantly because by the removal of any given line of the schedule, it is axiomatic, we contend, that the case the accused faces will inevitably be less serious. I accept not to any great extent, but still to some extent. Of course it depends on what part of the schedule in relation to the degree of seriousness. But, Your Honour, perhaps more fundamental in relation to this submission is how it impacts on the primary submission that I wish to make today in relation to this indictment. And that relates to the reference in Counts 1 and 2 to both Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats. Your Honour, the Defence submission in a nutshell, and I'll develop it in a few moments' time, that there is insufficient evidence which would allow the case to proceed beyond this point in relation to Bosnian Croats as opposed to Bosnian Muslims. And I'll come back, if I may, to the substantive issue in a moment but I just like to continue with what I'm saying about the old Rule and the new Rule. It may be that this Chamber will decide that the new Rule does not allow the Defence to make the submission in relation to Bosnian Croats in Counts 1 and 2 because it's -- to use an expression, it's tinkering with the indictment rather than dealing with a count in the way that the new Rule envisages. If that is right, a clearer case of prejudice to the accused would be hard to imagine, because it's apparent that the indictment in Counts 1 and 2 really makes two completely separate allegations and as I say I'm going to develop this in a moment. One is genocide against Bosnian Muslims and the other is genocide against Bosnian Croats. They are really two completely separate issues. Could I make it clear, Your Honour, I submit that both under the old Rule and the new Rule, this is a point the Defence are entitled to take at this stage of the proceedings. However, were the Court against me and say no, the new Rule does not now apply, I would submit strongly that that is, as I've already said, the clearest example of prejudice to the accused by the application of the new Rule. It's clearly far more fundamental than the schedule issue that I mentioned and I've relied upon earlier. Your Honour, could I begin so far as this is concerned, by simply outlining and perhaps accepting what the appropriate test is in relation to Rule 98 bis applications? Because it does appear that notwithstanding the change in the Rule, the law in relation to insufficiency of evidence -- perhaps I shouldn't say appears. I contend the law hasn't changed and a convenient enunciation of that -- of the law as applied in this Tribunal I would submit can be found in the Rule 98 bis Milosevic decision. Now, Your Honour, the Court is aware that of course was decided under the old Rule so Your Honour needs to bear that in mind and I provided that in the short handout. It's at the first page of the two page handout, says 3, application of Rule 98 bis, the law, and it's 8, "Rule 98 bis provides as follows." Now, Your Honour, I don't propose to read very much of this out. I simply take Your Honour to it because it sets out how the law developed here in the case of Jelisic and then and - excuse my pronunciation, it hasn't improved very much although I have tried very hard in that regard - Delalic. And then turning the page it in fact quotes quite extensively from an English case that I can pronounce called Galbraith, which is the modern English pronunciation on this very subject and there is a lengthy passage from I think it was Lord Lane's judgement at paragraph 12 of this decision. And then at paragraph 13 of this decision, the matter is summarised. And again, unless Your Honour wishes me to read through it paragraph by paragraph, it's there and I simply felt it my duty before I dealt with the substance of my submission, to outline what the test is. In fact if we look at the very last of the seven subcategories to paragraph 13 we see it says, "when in reviewing the evidence the Trial Chamber makes a finding that there is sufficient evidence, that is taken to mean that there is evidence on which a Trial Chamber could be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused." And of course the important word is could rather than would. I accept that and that's the point in hand now. But I'm not going to dwell on that. There is, I contend, no dispute about the correct test that the Chamber needs to apply at this stage. The test remains the same under both the old Rule and the new Rule and for what it's worth there are parts of this rather lengthy discussion that Judge Agius had with counsel where Judge Agius said exactly that. Moving on, the Chamber will, I suspect, also be relieved that for the presentation of my argument, I am not going to go in great detail through the elements of the offence of genocide. Clearly, in order to consider whether what I'm contending is right, namely there is insufficient evidence so far as Bosnian Croats are concerned, put another way I suppose what I am saying is that there is insufficient evidence on which a Trial Chamber could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused in relation to genocide of Bosnian Croats. Clearly, in order for the Chamber to consider that submission, it's going to have to look closely at the various elements of the offence of genocide because Your Honours, to state the obvious, the Court is going to have to consider genocide in relation to Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims. And the Chamber are aware that the elements that need to be proved by the Prosecution are, one, an intent; two, that is to destroy; three, in whole or in part; four, a national ethnical racial or religious group; and the fifth element is the use of the words "as such" in the article. And it may be worth briefly looking at Article 4 of the Statute to remind ourselves of what that says in subarticle 2: "Genocide means any of the following acts committed with the intent to destroy in whole or in part a national, ethnical, racial or religious group as such," and then it details the acts that can be used to prove the offence of genocide. Could I return briefly to why I submit that for all intents and purposes, Counts 1 and 2 are two different allegations. Could I say this, Your Honour? It may be that there is a technical argument that the Defence could have advanced, perhaps at an earlier stage rather than now, that the charge -- again if I could be excused using the English expression, is duplicitous. But the Defence take no point in that because clearly, were this Chamber to decide, again if I could use a colloquial English expression again, that my client had a case to answer in relation to both Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats so far as the offence of genocide is concerned, then in due course a reasoned judgement will be given in relation to the case as a whole and all parties will know where they stand. And so the fact that they are lumped together in one count perhaps doesn't matter a great deal. Having said that, that is no reason why the Court shouldn't consider them separately at this stage of the case. And, Your Honour, it's a very obvious point which perhaps I haven't made and I should have done, namely this: That it will make a significant difference for the presentation of the Defence case, if there is insufficiency of evidence so far as Bosnian Croats are concerned on the offence of genocide. I mean, it clearly is of real importance to the presentation of the Defence case, the ruling that is made so far as that is concerned. Because the Defence will know in relation to what is undoubtedly the most serious offence on this indictment where they stand so far as that allegation is concerned because I emphasise yet again they clearly are two distinct and separate allegations because they are two distinct and separate racial groups. And it's quite clear from the reading of Article 4(2) that the fact is the ethnic makeup of the group is of importance. And just perhaps -- whilst I'm developing that, could I contrast that if I may with all the other counts on the indictment, were I not to take the point, all the other counts talk -- and we could look at Count 3 by way of example, but they are all drafted in more or less the same way. Count 3, paragraph 18, two lines from the bottom of the version I've got, it talks about the preparation or execution of persecution of the Bosnian Muslim, Bosnian Croat or other non-Serb populations. Well, the point is this: That there it actually is not, I say, material to the count whether the Prosecution have proved the persecution is against Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Croats, because the nature of the article -- we could look at the article if need be, that the defendant is alleged to have transgressed, namely Article 5 so far as a crime against humanity is concerned. It's not material, it doesn't matter what the racial origin of the member of that group is. If one looks at Article 5, just by way of example, it talks about "persons responsible for the following when committed in armed conflict... and directed against any civilian population." So the particularisation by the Prosecution that they are Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims or other non-Serbs which I'm going to come to a bit later, but it doesn't -- is a particularisation which is ultimately material. In Count 1 and 2 the distinction between Croats and Muslims is fundamental and material to the offence. In other words, the nature of the racial group has to be charged because of the way Article 4 is understandably drafted. It's the whole essence of genocide, after all. I submit on behalf of my client that this is a case that has been presented to this Chamber over a considerable period of time of allegations of genocide against Bosnian Muslims. There is evidence of what I will term wrongdoings, perhaps even atrocities against Bosnian Croats, but in no meaningful sense can this trial be said, I contend, to be a trial involving the genocide of Bosnian Croats. And whilst what I'm saying there perhaps doesn't amount to a legal submission, the essence of the case is an important consideration and is something that I urge the Chamber to take into account even at this stage. Now, I went through the elements of the offence of genocide a little earlier. I am not going to deal with the thorny and difficult question of the law of intention in relation to the offence of genocide but I am in no way conceding that there is evidence as far as Bosnian Croats and the allegation of genocide is concerned which is capable of supporting the Prosecution's allegation. For ease of presentation, as much as anything else, I'm bound to say, I am not at this juncture dealing with that particular element of the offence. I would, however, like to say a few words about the element described as "to destroy" in the Article. The accused or the accused in concert with those he's alleged to be involved in a joint criminal enterprise with, must be proved to intend to destroy Bosnian Croats. I submit that evidence of a desire and/or intention to cause suffering and/or to discriminate is insufficient. It's our submission that the Prosecution must prove physical destruction. Not enough to prove that those involved in the joint criminal enterprise were simply involved in ethnic cleansing. It's submitted that what must be proved is an intention to destroy the Bosnian Croats in their physical or biological existence, and that has not been achieved by the Prosecutor in this case. Similarly, if I could turn to the use of the words, "in part" because clearly there is a case where the Prosecution allege both actually that there was genocide in part and that was the intention of the accused and those involved in the joint criminal enterprise. So far as in part is concerned, the Prosecution it's submitted must prove that the destruction of that part, if carried out, would have an impact on the whole group's survival. This can only be done when there is credible evidence that the destruction of that part could have an effect upon the survival of the group. And so far as Bosnian Croats are concerned again it's submitted that there is not sufficient evidence for this Chamber to allow that element of the count to proceed further. So, Your Honour, that really is my primary submission today. May return to it very briefly in my conclusion which will not be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. very far away. But could I move on to three matters where in discussion that I've had over the last few days with the Office of the Prosecutor, the parties have come to agreement and where, in fact, as much as anything for clarification, I'd like to draw some matters, if I may, to the Chamber's attention. The first is this: We spotted that there was an internal contradiction in the indictment because in paragraphs 15 and 16, paragraph 15 talks about the "partial destruction." In paragraph 16 it talks about an intent to destroy in part. But then in paragraph 17, the word "partial" is not used. It simply talks about "the destruction of these groups was affected by." Well of course that must be wrong because the Bosnian Croats weren't, in fact, destroyed so that must -- should read "partial destruction." But of more concern to the Defence was paragraph 28, if Your Honours would go to that, please. Because in paragraph 28, it talks about "all acts or omissions charged as genocide or complicity in genocide were committed with intent to destroy in whole or in part Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats, national, ethnical, racial or religious groups as such." We were concerned about the use of the words "in whole" because clearly paragraph 28 relates to intention. The earlier parts of the indictment talked about an intention to destroy both groups in part. And I'm grateful to the OTP because they have made it clear to me and I'm sure they will to the Chamber if a few moments' time that their case is an intention to destroy in part and that the words "in whole" shouldn't actually be there. Next, Your Honour, there was concern from the Defence, and I've alluded to these words in a different context a few moments ago, of the use in all counts, 3 to 8, not 1 and 2, rather illustrates the point I was making a moment ago, of the words, "or other non-Serb populations." In effect I asked the Prosecutor to clarify what was meant by the words "or other non-Serb populations." And they have helpfully indicated that those words are, I hope I can use the expression, meaningless in this indictment, that the allegations of persecutions, extermination and killing, deportation and inhumane acts relates only, if I can use the word advisedly, to Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats. And as I already said, and I mention it again simply to emphasise what I've said earlier, I make no submission so far as Bosnian Croats are concerned in relation to Counts 3 to 8. I accept the sufficiency of evidence for the purposes of this submission so far as those counts are concerned, and I've also been at pains, I hope, to explain why I say the ethnic or national character of the victims of those alleged crimes, namely Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims, doesn't actually matter, whereas it is the very essence of the offence of genocide. I simply mention that again. I hope to make clear what my position is and what my primary submission is today. Finally, in terms of clarification, in Count 3, there was some concern in paragraph 18 on the part of the Defence as to whether the Prosecution had in fact called sufficient evidence in relation to all the municipalities mentioned at the top of page 8, and I'm told the Prosecution concede that there isn't -- insufficient evidence so far as Rudo and Sipovo are concerned and they are not relying on those two municipalities. So I'm grateful for that. Well, Your Honour, before I conclude my submissions today, I've contended in the last few minutes that the Defence have been prejudiced by the change in the Rule, and in effect I've asked the Court to consider that as my first, if not my primary submission. However, if the Court took the view that there is no prejudice and there is no need in effect to go back and deal with this matter under the old Rule, then I contend that in any event the new Rule, which will clearly be the Rule that you would deal with and make a ruling under, does make a further fundamental change and it's this: It makes Rule 98 bis Chamber-driven rather than party-driven. And in other words, I contend, it is incumbent on the Trial Chamber to fully review the counts and be satisfied, to use again the English expression, that the accused has a case to answer on each and every count and of course, give reasons for that conclusion. The matter, if I may say, is well expressed by Judge Agius in the last passage of the Oric transcript that I would like to rely upon today. If Your Honour would look at the two-page -- it may be a three-page extract from the Oric judgement, the one that in the middle of the page says page 7854. At line 19, above, this is Judge Agius speaking, line 18, he says: "And you will also notice that the new Rule 98 bis motion does not say that at the close of the Prosecutor's case 'the Trial Chamber may,' but it says 'shall.' So the first message, or the first conclusion to be drawn on the face of it from the new Rule 98 bis is that it has become mandatory now for the Trial Chamber to embark on this Rule 98 bis acquittal exercise at the end of the Prosecutor's case and need not wait for the Defence to file or to make any application for the acquittal of the client. So that is point number one, and I would like you to understand it from the very beginning. "Next thing, it says 'by oral decision.' So you will immediately notice that what previously was essentially a written decision has now become an oral decision. Let me explain something which -- the only thing that I think is relevant in this context. The fact that we are now saying by oral decision does not in any way diminish or do away with the duty of the Trial Chamber to make sure that its oral decision is a reasoned one. Prior to the amendment in December 1998 there would have been a written decision, even in most cases as it was preceded by the oral decision. In both the oral decision and -- but particularly in the written decision, the decision to acquit or not to acquit was always motivated and the reason is not only because giving reasons decision is a matter of natural justice, it's a modern development in the area or in the concept of natural -- principles of natural justice, for those who believe in natural justice. And I skip the next few lines because he deals with the context and the concept, perhaps I should say, of natural justice. And then, at line 20, he deals with the right to appeal and the reason why a reasoned decision is important so far as that's concerned. At the bottom of the page, that is where it says page 7855, the learned Judge continues: "Appeals were dealt with and determined with the utmost celerity; and secondly, the case, the trial will not stop pending the determination of the appeal. For these same reasons, I need hardly, therefore, repeat to you that our oral decision will of course be a reasoned one, a reasoned one. So do not expect any surprises on -- in that context. And of course and after the hearing of the oral submission of the parties, basically this mean that you will both be given the opportunity to be heard, to make submissions, if you want to make submissions. No one will be forced to make submissions. And after then," I beg your pardon, "And after that, we are then expected by the new Rule 98 bis to enter a judgement of acquittal on any count there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction." What I take Judge Agius to be saying in that passage, Your Honour, is this: That regardless of whether the Defence make a submission, it's the duty of a Trial Chamber at this stage of the case, under the new procedure, to review the evidence and to be satisfied that the accused has a case to answer in relation to all the counts that he faces. And of course, if the Trial Chamber does conclude that he has a case to answer or indeed if he concludes that he doesn't have a case to answer, it's then incumbent upon the Trial Chamber to give a reasoned judgement so far as that is concerned. That's clear from the words of Judge Agius. I would adopt what the learned Judge was saying there and contend that if the court decides to proceed by way of the old Rule, I beg your pardon, by way of the new Rule, it's incumbent upon the Chamber at this stage to review all the evidence and give a full reasoned judgement in relation to all eight counts. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Let me first -- before we give an opportunity to the Prosecution to respond, perhaps after a break see whether there are any questions by the Bench at this moment for you so that we could -- at least also the Prosecution could take your answers into consideration while preparing its response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I would have one question for you in relation to Rule 6(D). You referred to the prejudice the accused might suffer under the new Rule. May I ask you whether any -- what right exactly is involved? Because Rule 6(D) reads "but shall not operate to prejudice the rights of the accused." Would -- well, let me try to give you an example. If, for example, the time limit for responding to motions would be cut back from, in general, from 14 days to 12 days, would that be -- could that rule not apply in any pending case because it would operate to prejudice the rights of the accused? You understand the question is whether there is a right to respond, or whether the 14 days' time limit is the specific right granted to an accused. So where to draw a line between -- well, I would say inconvenience caused by the change of a Rule and what rights might be envisaged when Rule 6(D) was drafted, because you -- prejudicial to the accused, prejudicial to the right of the accused. You understand, I hope, my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. And the best I can do in response is really I suppose reiterate one point that I made in particular, namely this: Firstly, were the Chamber to take the view that under the new rule my basic submission so far as Bosnian Croats was concerned was not permissible under the new rule a clearer example of a man's rights, man being deprived of his rights would be hard to imagine because it would mean that he would still is have a case to answer in relation to allegation of the utmost seriousness, and if that doesn't connotate a deprivation of a right, i.e. deprivation to make that submission, it's hard to imagine what else could be envisaged by the drafter of the Rule. But even if I'm wrong about that, I still contend that - or perhaps I should say not so much if I'm wrong about that but even if the Chamber was to take the view that I'm entitled to make the submission under the new Rule - the accused's rights, I contend are still affected by the fact that he's unable under the new Rule to go through the indictment line by line, almost letter by letter, in the way that the old Rule envisaged. That was a right that he had, a right he could exercise at this particular stage of the case, by motion, it's fair to say, rather than naturally in the way that the new Rule envisages. But I submit that that is a right and that right will -- has disappeared by reason of the Rule change. I recognise, if I may say, that the Rule change was implemented as much as anything for practical reasons but of course the practical reasons might impinge on rights and I submit that it does do exactly that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then ask you as that follow-up question, where is that right -- whether let's for example concentrate on the line by line going through not only through the indictment but also through the schedules. Let's say for example you would like to argue that there is no case to answer on execution and Ilijas of 18 Bosnian Muslims because there would be evidence only for 12 so therefore at least six should be taken out. Where is that right defined under the old Rule 98 bis? What I'm asking you is: Are you saying that the underlying reasons for amending the Rule would affect the practice as it had developed until then? Because where do I read in the old Rule that you could go in your motion line by line, apart from practice, perhaps, in some cases where you find in quite some detail that on some lines there is no evidence. So I'm trying to explore exactly what has changed, what rights were granted, what was practice rather than established right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, obviously I needed to look at the practice of the Tribunal when I began this particular exercise. In fact, though I found an older case, as good an example of any is the Milosevic Rule 98 bis decision because -- I have the whole decision here. If one looks at paragraph 309 at page 73 of the decision, there then follows in excess of 15 pages in table form of repetition, reproduction, perhaps I should say, the of the relevant parts of the schedule where each party has made submissions literally line by line so far as particular events that took place and box one it says, in fact -- of course the accused, Your Honour is aware is not represented in that case, box one says "the amici curiae submits"; box two says "the Prosecution submits"; and box three says "the Trial Chamber finds." And then in the fourth box, there is a reference to the evidence on the subject. So for example the one I'm looking at is a witness who I know has given evidence in this case, maybe by 92 bis, Professor Tabeau, as where the evidence could be found. So that's where the practice is clearly established. So far as the new Rule is concerned, they have not been very many cases that have got to this stage since it was brought into force in December of last year. The Oric case being the only one that I've examined. I don't know whether that -- I know in Halilovic, no Rule 98 bis submission was made and then I don't know what happened, I rather suspect, I can't swear to this, that the Chamber didn't undertake the task that I've invited it to undertake pursuant to the very last submission that I made. So the new Rule is not tried and tested I think it would be fair to say, Your Honour, and that's why I looked particularly at what Judge Agius said, and as Your Honour knows far better than I do, he of course was chairman or president of the Rules Committee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for these answers, Mr. Josse. Since there are no other questions to you at this moment from the Bench, I suggest that we'll have a break. I'm looking to you, Mr. Tieger. Do you know how much time approximately you would need also to determine how much time there would be available for you to take for preparing your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would say that certainly no extraordinary break is needed. So whatever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour. I should mention, as I was intending to at the beginning of my submissions that both parties have had the benefit, as counsel has mentioned, of discussion. That has enabled us to focus on the matters genuinely at issue and that's one of the reasons why no lengthier break is required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then adjourn until quarter past 12 and then the Prosecution will have the opportunity to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I mention one matter? I do have here, and it was in the e-mail that I sent to the legal officer yesterday, Your Honour, the whole of the discussion, if I put it, that Judge Agius had with counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- I said -- the Chamber highly appreciates that you indicated what material you would use and I've got in the Oric case, page 7847 and up until 7878, and I hope that Defence is not disappointed that I did not give a similar lecture as Judge Agius did in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but simply bearing in mind the question that Your Honour had asked, I think it may be worth Your Honour and the Chamber reading that exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. We will adjourn until quarter past 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, just before the break, I said that I would give you an opportunity to respond, but I would rather say to make whatever submissions the Prosecution would like to make also in response to what the Defence has submitted until now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution submissions will for the reasons I indicated earlier be essentially limited to a response to the submissions the Court heard earlier this morning. Before moving on to address the basic submission offered by Mr. Josse, perhaps I should take up the three clarification matters he addressed and largely confirm those, with one small clarification with respect to the allegations of other non-Serb populations that he spoke of. He spoke of three things, the municipality issue, and the partial destruction issue, and then he raised the question of the allegations of, for example, persecutions against Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Croats or other non-Serbs. I would indicate, as the Court is aware, that there has indeed been evidence of crimes committed against other non-Serbs, in particular, as I recall, Albanians and Kosovars and nothing I say at this point is intended to gainsay the sufferings endured by those particular people but it is correct to say, as Mr. Josse indicated, that the charges alleged in the indictment are directed toward crimes committed against the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat populations, and that's the thrust of the Prosecution case. That's the emphasis of the Prosecution case. And with respect to other non-Serbs, the Prosecution is -- has not intended to make those crimes part of its presentation. Let me then move on, Your Honours, to focus on the thrust of the submissions made by Mr. Josse. It's the Prosecution's submission that, in fact, Rule 98 bis, in its current incarnation, does not countenance a line-by-line review of the indictment, which would embrace counts 1 and 2 and an attempt to parse out portions of those counts, and that this does not entail the deprivation of any substantive right, as I will explain in a moment. Mr. Josse points out that if 98 bis doesn't permit such a review, in the case of the allegations contained in Rule -- in Counts 1 and 2, then there will be some asserted impact on the accused. We would simply point out that the proper remedy for the formulation in Counts 1 and 2 would have been a motion under Rule 72 challenging the form of the indictment which should have been made a long time ago. The fact that Rule 98 bis in fact does not encompass the same provisions that another rule of the indictment which was not invoked in a timely fashion, does, does not change the fact that Rule 98 bis, number 1, doesn't permit the line-by-line review sought by the Defence, with respect to the allegations in Counts 1 and 2, and also does not result in a deprivation of any substantive right as a result. Now, the Court inquired about the nature of that right, as referred to in Rule 6. The Prosecution would submit that the first stopping point for an examination of whether or not a right is involved would be Article 21 of the Statute which enumerates rights and we would further submit that the right asserted by the Defence is not to be found there. Now, assuming that it's appropriate to go beyond Article 21 in determining whether or not a substantive right within the meaning of Rule 6 is involved, it would be then appropriate to look at the nature of the asserted right itself, and in this case, we would be looking at the right of a mid-trial review of some sort. And in that connection I would point the Court to the decision on motion for judgement of acquittal that the Defence has already alluded to of 16 June 2004, which discusses the foundation of the mid-trial review, the no case to answer, in paragraph 11. As I think the Court will see, the critical aspect, or as the Milosevic Chamber said, crucial to an understanding of the no case to answer procedure, is the common-law distinction between the role of the judge and the role of the jury, and that is, it arises from the judge's oversight of another fact-finding body and the common law's concern that the case will go to the jury, the jury may act on an emotional basis in making a decision that is not founded on the actual evidence, and it seeks to have the judge in that case balance the interests between usurping the judge's role and precluding an emotional determination by the jury which is not compatible with the -- with a strict review of the evidence. That distinction is clearly missing here, and then that rather clearly I think accounts for the fact that the no case to answer rule did not exist when this institution was formed, did not exist in the 1994 rules and was in fact not adopted until 1998. Now, the adoption of the Rule in 1998 the Prosecution we would submit was not a reflection of the determination that somehow a substantive right had been overlooked when the Tribunal Rules of Procedure and Evidence were initially adopted, and had been overlooked in quite a number of subsequent years, and I think that is borne out by the fact that the ICC, as the Court can see in Judge Robinson's dissent in the same opinion of June 2004, did not adopt any provision for a no case to answer. Prosecution would submit that that is a reflection of the determination that this is a procedure which is -- which arises from a uniquely common-law system and is not required in a system where the judges who would be asked to make the mid-term determination are in fact the judges who are making the final determination. But let's assume even for the sake of argument that Rule 98 bis does reflect a substantive right of some sort. Then the question becomes: What is that right and what is its relationship to a demand that it embrace a line-by-line review of the indictment? Well part of that answer is surely found in the title of 98 bis itself. It's an acquittal provision. And that means an acquittal of the basic charges that the accused faces. As Judge Agius himself said in the Oric case to which counsel has alluded, charges and counts, the current formulation, are essentially the same and viewed as the same in common-law jurisdictions, and certainly when it's linked to the notion of acquittal, it indicates quite clearly that the notion of a line-by-line review is something quite different. It is for that reason, we would submit, that the distinction was made in the course of the discussion about 98 bis in the same Milosevic case to which we've been referring, between the Rule itself and the practice that had developed in the Tribunal. And in that connection, I would refer the Court to paragraph 13 of the Milosevic decision, where the Court identifies and distinguishes between the sufficiency of evidence to sustain a conviction on a charge, which is Rule -- which is what Rule 98 bis according to that same decision talks about, and the practice of the Tribunal, which had been up to that point to consider the sufficiency of the evidence as it pertains to elements of a charge, whether it was set out in separate paragraphs or in scheduled items. Those are two different things, the dictates and mandates and terms of the Rule and the practice that for whatever reason had developed around it, a practice that I think the Court is aware had come increasingly to be viewed with concern and to be subject to criticism. In short, the Rule 98 bis in either permutation never dictated in any sense a line-by-line determination of the indictment but for whatever reason that practice had developed as part of the procedure, at least in some cases, which accompanied the 98 bis determination. I think there is a consensus here that that is no longer the case and that does not appear to be disputed. What is at issue is the concern raised by Mr. Josse that somehow the allegations in Counts 1 and 2 should now be embraced by 98 bis because they seem significant enough in the Defence's view to require some remedial attention, that that should not -- that situation should not exist and should be addressed in some manner by the Rules, and again, we would submit that it is addressed by the Rules. It's addressed by Rule 72, which identifies the opportunity for the -- for either party, well, for the Defence, to challenge the form of the indictment at a much earlier stage of the proceeding. For whatever reason that was to not done and that was the appropriate remedy for the - if one was indeed appropriate - for the concern raised by the Defence. Now, finally -- well, not finally, Your Honour, but let me say let's assume however for the purposes of this discussion that 98 bis does require or permit a parsing out of Counts 1 and 2 and therefore a need to focus on the quantum of evidence concerning genocide against Bosnian Croats. It's the Prosecution's submission that ample evidence has been adduced during the course of this case to support that parsed-out aspect of Counts 1 and 2. Indeed, the Defence submission seems to be predicated on the general notion that a clear distinction has arisen during the course of this case between the objectives toward and the treatment of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats. The Prosecution's submission is that while there is a demographic difference between the two groups, a numerical discrepancy that has clearly resulted in a greater number of references to Bosnian Muslims in this case, that the objectives toward and the treatment of the two groups were fundamentally the same for purposes of this motion and I would like to explain that in further detail. First of all, without going into a lengthy discussion of the evidence adduced in the course of this case, I think it's -- I can begin by saying generally that the persecutory campaigns that are at the heart of this case emerged from the intention of the Bosnian Serb leadership and forces, according to the evidence, to secure Serbian ethnic territory in their determination, to separate from the other two nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And which was the first and most important goal of the strategic objectives, as the accused himself said at the 16th Bosnian Serb Assembly session. And on that occasion, in identifying that goal and its primary importance, he also noted explicitly that it was about separation from the other two national communities, meaning the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats. And as we'll see, the perspective on the view of and the treatment of Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims was not meaningfully different, at least not meaningfully different for purposes of this motion. As Radovan Karadzic said on that same occasion, the first such goal is separation from the other two national communities. Now, both of those national communities, both the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, were regarded as enemies. As Dr. Karadzic said, this is about separation from those who are our enemies and who have used every opportunity especially in this century to attack us and who would continue with such practices if we were to stay together in the same state. In discussing the common enemy, General Mladic, on the -- or on that same occasion, the 12th of May 1992, at the 16th Bosnian Serb Assembly session, also talked about both the Muslim and Croat people in identifying the enemy. And he said: "The enemy has attacked with all its might from all directions, and it is a common enemy, regardless whether it is the Muslim hordes or Croatian hordes. It is our common enemy." And as Mr. Krajisnik noted on that same date, "It will be possible to solve this thing with Muslims and Croats, only by war." And we've heard a great deal of evidence about how that war was waged and against whom it was waged. I would note that there was no question in the eyes of those who were -- of representatives of the international community who were present in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time about the fact that the efforts to secure territory through ethnic cleansing and through persecutory campaigns were waged against both Muslims and Croats and I would point the Court, for example, to the testimony of Ambassador Okun, who spoke, for example, about the impact of the -- and implications of the Bosnian Serb insistence that Serbian ethnic territories inhabited Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. by other nations would be subject to the determination of the plebiscite. And I'll paraphrase what he said. He hypothesised at opstina with 10.000 inhabitants, 5.000 Bosnian Muslims, 3.000 Bosnian Serbs, 2.000 Bosnian Croats, 10.000 in total, and discuss what would happen if a majority of the Serbs in that municipality, let's say 2.000 of the inhabitants of that municipality voted to be part of the joined territories of the Bosnian Serb authorities, despite the fact that the 7.000 others, the majority of people in the municipality, were against that. And he asked rhetorically the question: What was going to happen to those 7.000 people? They weren't going to disappear by some magic trick. He also discussed the provision in the Bosnian Serb constitution that Serbian ethnic territory included the -- that territory on which Serbs were a minority allegedly because of the genocide of World War II. And again he asked the question: What was going to happen to the other people? What about the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats? Again they were linked. And when Ambassador Okun described his awareness, either by being on the ground or by hearing it from other are international observers who had personally seen it of ethnic cleansing when he described bringing it directly to the attention of the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Mr. Krajisnik; when he described the forcible expulsion, the burning down of villages, the confinement in detention camps and concentration camps, he referred to both Muslims and Croats. And I would draw the court's attention to pages 4187 to 4189, 4252 through 4253 and other portions of his testimony surrounding that area. I would also note that this was openly acknowledged and the same linkage, the same focus on the common enemy and the treatment of the common enemy could be seen in passages from subsequent sessions of the Bosnian Serb assembly itself. And I would note in that connection, as a couple of examples, the 17th session, where representative Milanovic stated openly that we have a, "We have a huge problem with captured people of other nationalities. We have hundreds and thousands of these prisoners." And then he went on to mention who those national its were, Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Croats and others. At the 22nd session held in November of 1992, when there it was a discussion about the draft law on citizenship, one of the representatives complained about the possible implications of that draft law, noting that it included a provision that citizenship could be acquired by birth in the territory of Republika Srpska, "Which in fact means that all Muslims and Croats who have been expelled have the citizenship of Republika Srpska." Again, the linkage of the two groups, the identical treatment of the same groups for the same reason. And when we look closer at some of the municipalities - and I'm not going to take the Court's time with all of them, just I'll focus on a few - we can see that a more micro examination of the individual municipalities bears out the comments at the Bosnian Serb Assembly and the observations and conclusions of the representatives of the international community. I would begin with, for example, the adjudicated facts on Prijedor. When it comes to the adjudicated facts concerning the demand for surrender of weapons, the attacks on villages, the various restrictions that were imposed, including the restrictions on freedom of movement, the propaganda and the ethnic insults that were leveled against people and that had a further role in terrorising them, the religious institutions that is were targeted for destruction, the confinement in camps in which many killings occurred and in which severe mistreatment was commonplace, we see in all those adjudicated facts that that campaign is leveled against both Muslims and Croats, again for the reasons stemming back to the pronouncements made by Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik at the 16th assembly session. If we want to look in particular at how Croat villages were treated, we can -- we need look no further than the testimony of KRAJ 336 from Kresevo. It was a Croat village in the so-called Brdo region of the Prijedor municipality which consisted of approximately 120 houses. Like the rest of the Brdo region, it was attacked and cleansed in the latter part of July 1992 in an attack which ran roughly, I think, from July 21st to July 24th and I think the attack on Kresevo was on July 24th. That small, relatively small village consisting of approximately 120 houses, was attacked by Serbian forces, Bosnian Serb forces. 68 people were murdered in that attack and the rest were rounded up and expelled from the region after a period of confinement. That community of Kresevo along with what ultimately turned out to be the remainder of the Bosnian Croat community in Prijedor was essentially decimated. I should also note that the partial destruction of the Bosnian Croat community in Prijedor and elsewhere was not simply numerical, that is based on the numbers of people killed, it was also selective and targeted. As the Court is aware, that is one of the factors to be considered in determining whether or not a genocide has occurred. I would in that connection remind the Court of the comments of the Minister of Health at the 16th assembly session on the 12th of May 1992, who said, "Have we chosen the option of war or the option of negotiating? I say this with a reason and I must instantly add: Knowing who our enemy is, how perfidious they are, how they cannot be trusted until they are physically, militarily destroyed and crushed, which of course implies eliminating and liquidating their key people, I do not hesitate in selecting the first option, the option of war." And in that connection, I would remind the Court of the testimony of Mr. Sejmenovic, who was here briefly as a 92 bis cross-examination witness but whose testimony from earlier cases was admitted. And he was asked on an earlier occasion in respect of the leadership of the SDA in Prijedor, what happened to the leaders of the SDA after the takeover by the SDS? And Mr. Sejmenovic went on to discuss the attack on parts of Prijedor and then said, afterwards, almost the entire leadership of the SDA, its members were captured. They were either killed or they were classified as missing for a while. A very small number of them managed to escape in time or hide somewhere." He was then asked about the fate of the leaders of the HDZ, the leaders of the Bosnian Croats, and he said, "I know that a similar fate also befell leaders of the HDZ." That is the -- there was selective targeting of the Bosnian Croat group in addition to the numbers of Bosnian Croats who were killed in attacks, killed in camps, subjected to forms of mistreatment and abuse on a wide scale that resulted in their deaths. Now, all of those are factors that have been identified in various cases as reflecting circumstances from which the intent required for genocide may be adduced. And those include the seriousness of the discriminatory acts, the general political doctrine giving rise to those acts that could be found as early as the Karadzic and Mladic Rule 61 decision in 1996; the destruction or attacks on cultural and religious property that could be found in the Krstic case; the destruction or attacks on houses belonging to members of the group, again the Krstic case; the desired destruction of a more limited number of persons selected for the impact that their disappearance would have on the ability of the group to survive, that's found in the Jelisic trial judgement and embraces one of the factors I just discussed. Now, although I indicated I wouldn't -- I'd attempt not to focus unduly on too many municipalities, I would probably be helpful if I mentioned just a couple of others because the pattern against Bosnian Croats in the same manner and for the same reasons that Bosnian Muslims were attacked is reflected in many other municipalities and I'm just going to mention a few. I'll begin with Brcko and start with Witness KRAJ 213. He said that the Bosnian Serbs wanted only a 5 per cent of the total population of Brcko to remain. Only Bosniaks and Croats were referred to. That would be enough people for them to sweep the streets and to work in night shifts. He talked about mass graves. There were no signs to show that people, that is those who were in mass graves, were killed by shells. They were all killed in a bestial way only because they were Muslims or Croats. We could can turn also in Brcko to KRAJ 214. He discussed the fact that it was -- that the SDS intention to reduce the population of non-Serbs to below 10 per cent was -- and that that was known. And that reduction of the population included Bosniaks and included Croats as targets of this reduction. He also described some individuals who were killed, including people who were killed because they were Croats and, in particular, including one victim who was killed not just because he was Croat but because he was a prominent Croat. We could also turn to the municipality of Teslic, for example, and the testimony of Mr. Petrovic. He discussed the fact that there were those who were precluded from working in the MUP or in the police department. Those were Muslims and Croats. He talked about people being forced out of jobs; again, Muslims and Croats. The destruction of property by the Red Berets; same thing, Croats and Muslims again. The destruction of mosques, and the destruction of Catholic churches. KRAJ 484 from Teslic talked about Muslims and Croats detained, approximately 250 of them and how those Muslims and Croats were taken from the hangar, they heard many screams and many of them were never seen again. I could also turn quickly as just another example, to Sanski Most, and if you look at the testimony of KRAJ 196 or KRAJ 565 you see restrictions, persecutions, mistreatment, again not directed just as Muslims but directed at both groups in the same manner. And I would also note the testimony of KRAJ 628, who said, all the Muslim and Croat villages were ethnically cleansed of the non-Serbs not only in Sanski Most but throughout Krajina. Again, Your Honour, although I don't think the Court needs to reach that issue for the reasons I mentioned in the earlier portion of my submission, I re-emphasise that the evidence amply demonstrates that even if the kind of line-by-line reading or review of that portion of the indictment on which Mr. Josse has focused is permitted, that the -- there is ample evidence to support the allegation and the motion under Rule 98 bis regarding that limited portion of the indictment to which they have directed their attention should be denied. If I may have just a moment? That concludes my submissions, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse before I give you an opportunity to make any further submissions, as you would like, I noticed that there seems to be quite a different view on Counts 1 and 2, your perception being that the joint criminal enterprise or at least the crimes covered by it would be 2(A) genocide against Bosnian Muslims, 2(B) being genocide against the Bosnian Croats, whereas it seems that the perception of the Prosecution is that genocide was committed against groups - the plural - that could be identified by them being Muslims and of Croat and Muslim ethnicity but taken together, which of course raises the issue about how a group should be defined, what are subgroups, whether you could combine two groups which seems to me not exactly the same but could be taken together in contrast to another group still defined by nationality or religion or by ethnicity. That seems to be apart from the issue of whether there is evidence seems to be one of the basic disagreements between the parties, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure there is quite as much disagreement as perhaps my comments inadvertently implied or as the Court is suggesting. We certainly agree with the Defence to this extent, and that is that the -- that Counts 1 and 2 allege genocide and they allege it -- and that genocide, they -- those allegations assert, was established on the basis of a genocide committed against Bosnian Muslims and on the basis of a genocide committed against Bosnian Croats. The two groups are not lumped together. And in that sense I would concede that the Defence is correct, there is a genocide against Bosnian Muslims alleged, a genocide against Bosnian Croats. The Defence concern is that the accused could be found guilty if, for example, well, if their submission, if there is a -- if the Court finds a genocide against Bosnian Muslims but not a genocide against Bosnian Croats, that's true, but we assert that the remedy for that existed long ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that raises a totally different question, Mr. Tieger. How possibly could the Defence have raised the issue that there was not sufficient evidence presented for that part of the genocide charges, whether you call that Count 1 genocide against Croats and genocide also in a cumulative nature, or whether you say Count A(1) is a genocide against Bosnian Muslims, Count 1(B)? I mean, of course it becomes a bit of a play of what's 1(A) and what's 1(B) and what's 1 and 2. At what stage, because you're referring to the pre-trial stage -- how could they have possibly raised the issue that not sufficient evidence has been presented by the Prosecution to prove genocide against Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course that's correct, it's a logical impossibility that they could have presented such an argument before any evidence was produced in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're nevertheless suggesting that they had other remedies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My point is that in a jury system, for example, the concern might be that the jury would somehow confuse or conflate the two groups and use evidence against one to bolster evidence against another and would therefore seek under a provision similar to our Rule 72, to have the amendment modified to make these separate counts. That it would be the allegation. Now, in a system -- in a judge-based system, the court will make appropriate findings that preclude that risk. That may well be why no such challenge was raised under Rule 72 earlier but that was the sense in which I meant it could have been addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least it becomes clearer and clearer to me. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had a chance to discuss this at some length over the last days with Mr. Tieger and he and I are in broad agreement about this. Could I illustrate the point even more starkly if I may? It's my submission that in Counts 1 and 2, there really are two different offences. Let's just call it Count 1 genocide because it's similar. But clearly, there would be a pair of counts representing the alternative, complicity in genocide, and the two offences are one, genocide against Bosnian Muslims and the others is genocide against Bosnian Croats. And perhaps I didn't make it clear enough earlier but I contrasted that quite deliberately with the other counts on the indictment where I make no complaint about, if I can adopt Your Honours' expression or perhaps my learned friend's expression, them being lumped together. We don't complain about that partly because of the reading of the Article, because again, using an English expression, it's a material averment that the Prosecution should have to prove that the genocide is committed against a national ethnical, racial or religion group and ironically, Your Honour, the only element in relation to genocide or alleged genocide against Bosnian Croats that the Defence concede is proved is that they are a national group. I went through the five elements earlier and that's the one element that I accept is proved. It would be ludicrous if I was to assert that Bosnian Croats weren't a group under the Article. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was more a misunderstanding of the Prosecution's position than a misunderstanding of your position, as a matter of fact, that caused me to ask that question to Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At one point, and this in fact now leads conveniently on to what I want to say by way of response, at one point it occurred to me that I could be in the ludicrous and unfortunate position of asking for these counts to be split because certainly in common-law jurisdictions that I know about, the remedy would be in fact to create further counts, because there, the jury will simply return a verdict of guilty or not guilty. And if the verdict is guilty, the judge who is then going to sentence the accused would need to know the basis of that finding. That isn't a problem here, I readily accept, because if this Chamber finds my client does have a case to answer in relation to both Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats, then in due course, I know we will get reasons as to whether he is found guilty of one, both, not guilty of one, not guilty of both so it actually doesn't matter so far as that is concerned but. It of course does make a very real practical difference as to where the case goes from now. And in specific response to what Mr. Tieger has just said, I contend that the Prosecution's primary assertion is that it's too late because the point wasn't taken under Rule 72. That simply cannot be right both in fairness and indeed in practicality, the practicality being the Defence case which will now follow. And there is no difficulty, I submit, with the Trial Chamber dealing with the submission, in other words not lumping the two together at this stage. There is no difficulty with it. And if nothing else, what perhaps we can all agree upon is that the new Rule 98 bis is designed to achieve a practical and real result rather than an artificial result which it so often used to do perhaps in the past. But, Your Honour, if the Defence are wrong about that, if I'm wrong about what I have just said, that emphasises more clearly than anything else why the rights of my client have been prejudiced by the change of the Rules. So I submit, if I can put it this way, that I win both ways on that point, either under the old rule or the new rule and why, if I'm wrong that the new Rule doesn't cater for it the old Rule must come into play and we need to go backwards, unfortunately. So far as the substance of Mr. Tieger's assertions, so far as the evidence is concerned, I was at pains to point out, and if I didn't do so before I certainly do now, that there is evidence and perhaps quite a lot of it, that relates to the maltreatment, discrimination of Bosnian Croats, evidence perhaps of war crimes including very unpleasant murders, but I submit that on any reading of the evidence as a whole, applying the correct test, the evidence does not amount to genocide, bearing in mind the elements that require proving. By way of example, Mr. Tieger doing the best he can, cites a passage from another trial that's been admitted in this case from Mr. Sejmenovic, and as one line that he relies upon, which relates to a particular type of discrimination, I think choice of leaders of Bosnian Croats being selected for discrimination and perhaps murder. But really, in a scale of a case like this, to rely on that one piece of evidence illustrates the Defence's point that genocide is simply not made out. I contend in conclusion that the Trial Chamber needs to grapple with these matters and ask itself whether it really wants to widen still further the ambit of the offence of genocide and ask itself look at the elements that need to be proved and ask itself whether in fact they are proved to the sufficient standard at this stage in relation to Bosnian Croats and the Defence contend resoundingly that the answer to that is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I have one question for you and that's the following. Apart from a couple of lines of the evidence, I think what Mr. Tieger also tried to do hard is to draw the attention of the Chamber to those portions of the evidence in which -- which would suggest that the treatment of the one group would not be distinguishable from the other group, so therefore he did not only or not primarily pay attention to the ill-treatment because that's what the Chamber understood well, you could say well, ill-treating people, even if you murder people that doesn't mean that you are fulfilling all the elements of genocide. But I think what Mr. Tieger tried hard - whether he has succeeded or not he'll find out at a later stage - but he tried hard to draw attention to the fact that on the political level the groups were treated equally. And if I do understand him well, is that he suggests with that that by treating them equally would mean that what happens on the grounds with one group which numerically certainly is far larger than the other group, would nevertheless allow for some inferences to make in respect of the smaller group. First of all, Mr. Tieger, if I misunderstood your arguments, please tell us now so that Mr. Josse doesn't have to respond to any misunderstood arguments. But if I understood your argument well then I would invite Mr. Josse to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would have done so, Your Honour. Thanks for the opportunity and the Court's understanding is essentially correct, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, then you're invited to respond to that element as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour has heard the evidence in this case over very many months and again, if I could be excused stating the obvious and I'm not seeking here to make a jury speech, the qualitative and quantitative evidence in relation to Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats is so enormously different that I don't need to emphasise it beyond what I have already said, and Mr. Tieger carefully, meticulously and I accept fairly has chosen parts of the evidence which suggest discrimination and in some cases equal discrimination against Bosnian Croats. But overall, as I've already said, the quality and quantity of the evidence varies enormously, and it isn't just a case of intention, although I submit that so far as intention is concerned, the Prosecution haven't made out its case, it's also a matter of the actuality of the situation.
